title: Don't wait to be rich
hook: many would have reached wisdom if they hadn't thought they'd need to be rich first

segments.voice: Yesterday's word was Epicurus, and Seneca's point: philosophy lives in deeds, not words. Your line was not words, shape.

Once the kids are older. Once I pay off the card. Once work calms down. Once I have the right shoes, the right desk, the right app. Then I'll start. Plenty of plans hang on a sentence like that, and the thing they're waiting for keeps moving. Lucilius had one too. He told Seneca he'd devote himself to philosophy properly once he'd put enough money aside to live on. Seneca's seventeenth letter is his reply, and it's not gentle.
screen: `ONCE THE KIDS ARE OLDER.` → `ONCE I HAVE ENOUGH.` → `DON'T WAIT TO BE RICH.`

segments.voice: Lucilius wants to build up savings before giving himself to the study of how to live. Sounds sensible. Seneca tells him to throw that plan out. If you're wise, hurry toward a sound mind now. Riches, he says, have shut many people off from wisdom. They meant to get rich first and study how to live afterward, and the afterward never came. The getting-ready becomes the whole life; the money always needs a little more. Then he praises a poor person's freedom. When the war trumpet sounds, the poor know they aren't the ones under attack. When a house is on fire, they look for the way out, not for what to carry. When a poor person sets out to sea, no crowd of servants fills the dock. Hunger costs little; fussiness costs a lot. Nature asks for very little. If you want room for your mind, either be poor, or live as if you were. He closes with Epicurus again: for many, getting rich didn't end their troubles; it only changed them. The study of wisdom, Seneca says, can't do you good without care for simple living, and simple living is a poverty you choose. That choice is open on any budget: a notebook instead of a course, a walk instead of a gym, five quiet minutes instead of a retreat.
screen: `FIRST SAVINGS, THEN WISDOM?` · `THE GETTING-READY BECOMES THE LIFE.` · `THE POOR TRAVEL LIGHT.` · `SIMPLE LIVING, CHOSEN.` · then, large: `START POOR.`

segments.voice: Name one thing you've been waiting to begin until conditions are right, and what you've told yourself you need first. Then ask what you could do with exactly what you have, today, and make it tiny: one page, one call, one stretch. Notice how small the first step really is.
Simple living. Seneca's seventeenth letter: a poverty you choose, open on any budget, so you don't have to wait to be rich. Today's word.
Your line: start poor. What's already in your hands is enough to begin. Day four hundred fifty-one, done.

howItsDone: Following Seneca, some people begin a practice of reflection or study right away with simple means, rather than waiting for savings, time off or better conditions.

notes: Editor review 2026-10-01: cut 'one of the richest men in Rome' (unsourced superlative, and a near-repeat of day 452's 'honest twist') and the teaching of tomorrow's letter; the fourth turn now follows 17.5 (frugality as voluntary poverty); 'almost everyone', 'most good things' and the told feeling in the practice removed; myth and trapdoor now come from Letter 17; On the Happy Life source dropped.

Checked against Gummere (Wikisource), Letter 17: 17.1 Lucilius wants his estate settled first; 17.3 'Riches have shut off many a man from the attainment of wisdom', the trumpet, the cry of fire, and the poor man going to sea with no retinue on the wharves; 17.4 hunger costs little, squeamishness much; 17.5 'either be a poor man, or resemble a poor man'; 17.9 nature demands but little; 17.11 Epicurus on riches as a change, not an end, of troubles. All paraphrased. Reviewer fixes: the earlier draft had sailors throwing cargo overboard in a storm and 'bread and water', neither of which is in Letter 17 (bread and water is Letters 18 and 25), and stated the index line as a counterfactual ('many would have reached wisdom if...') that the letter does not contain; the teach now follows 17.3.
